prize_parts.citation: for methods to estimate demand, competition and market power in differentiated-product industries, and for frameworks for dynamic industry analysis

statement.case_for: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (BLP) turned demand estimation for differentiated products into a usable empirical tool. The method handles endogenous prices and consumer heterogeneity, and it recovers elasticities, markups and welfare effects from market data. Pakes's dynamic industry work extends the same approach to entry, investment and industry evolution. Merger review, antitrust, and applied work in trade, health and environmental policy now use these tools routinely, so the influence on research and policy can be traced directly. The contribution is also mature. The core work dates from the mid-1990s and has been applied and extended for roughly three decades. Nobody has raised a scientific objection to this ballot in the opening round. Its main weakness is attribution, not importance or timing. I still rank it first after reading the colleagues' openings. B022 and B012 are strong, but I do not think they are better on merit.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is attribution. The ballot credits seven names, so a three-person cap leaves out real contributors, above all Bresnahan, whose earlier work on demand and market power in differentiated-product markets is a genuine precursor. Two further concerns apply. First, BLP-style estimates depend on functional-form, instrument and equilibrium assumptions, and as someone from the design-based tradition I take the credibility debate between structural and reduced-form approaches seriously. Second, only four members ranked this ballot, so it faces a real coordination problem. The Committee may also hesitate over a second methods-oriented prize soon after 2021. B022 is the stronger fallback on breadth and on its link to clear policy questions.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B022 first but would credit only Autor and Hanson. He treats Dorn and Katz as more junior or tied to other bodies of work, and he notes that task-model theory owes much to people outside the credited set.
responses.response: I agree that the task-framework credit is diffuse and extends beyond the credited names. That is partly why I rank B022 third and not first. I would not drop Dorn, though. The China-shock papers are joint work by Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and a citation built on the trade-shock evidence and local labour-market adjustment is cleaner with all three. Seniority is not the right test. I also share Teorell's concern about debate over magnitudes and persistence, including shift-share identification. I accept that the central findings have held up, so B022 stays my first alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B014 first. She argues that population-scale administrative data combined with credible quasi-experimental design on a big question meets the standard of new data plus an explanatory framework, and that replication across countries has helped.
responses.response: I am sympathetic, because register-based quasi-experimental work is close to my own research. I still rank B014 fifth for three reasons. The central results are about a decade old. The causal neighbourhood-exposure estimates are still being tested and extended. The credit is spread across a large team, so the three-name limit forces contested exclusions. Hassler's point that earlier mobility literatures exist also bears on what exactly the prize would name. For me the question is whether this is a conceptual advance or mainly a measurement and data advance. If the Committee answers that clearly and the replication record keeps growing, my ranking could move up.

responses.point: Krusell also ranks B029 first. He asks whether the prize would be read as a methods prize or a prize for economic discoveries, and he treats Bresnahan and Reiss as adjacent contributors.
responses.response: I share the concern, but I think it is manageable. A citation should name what the methods made measurable: market power, substitution patterns, welfare and industry dynamics. That ties the award to economic findings, not to estimators alone, as the 2021 prize was framed around causal questions. On Bresnahan, I am less sure than my opening suggested. His earlier work on differentiated-product competition is a real claim. I still keep the BLP trio because the estimation framework that spread across fields is theirs, but I flag this as the place where the Committee should be most careful.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B029 third with the same trio. He notes that the seven-name list implies diffuse credit and asks whether Bresnahan should displace one of the BLP co-authors.
responses.response: I agree that the seven-name list shows how diffuse the credit is. I would not displace Berry or Levinsohn. Berry's inversion step and the BLP estimation procedure are what made the approach implementable, and Levinsohn is a co-author of the core paper. Replacing either with Bresnahan would change the citation toward earlier conceptual work and away from the estimation tool that was adopted. I accept that this is a judgement call and that a reasonable member could weigh it differently.

uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan's claim on the demand-side framework is strong enough to change the three-name attribution.
Whether enough members will see structural IO estimation as a discovery-level contribution; only four members ranked this ballot.
How much weight the Committee should give to sensitivity of structural estimates to identifying assumptions, relative to the design-based evidence in B022.
My account of the credit split rests on general knowledge and the supplied openings, and I have not independently verified it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My institutional overlap with Hassler and Krusell at Stockholm University is not a co-authorship, and it does not touch any shortlisted candidate's work.
